newsitem.title: UK: Gold Outlook-Move likely, but direction less clear.
newsitem.headline: Gold Outlook-Move likely, but direction less clear.

text.p: Gold prices were forecast to make a move this week after spending last week in a range of barely two dollars, according to dealers and analysts.
However, there was some doubt on direction given the expiry of over the counter (OTC) options later on Monday and any latent reaction generated by the G7 meeting at the weekend.
Early Monday prices were barely changed from Friday.
"There could be some volatility in the market early in the week but it will be difficult to know whether that is from the option expiry or from statements coming out of the G7," one analyst said.

One reason gold was trapped in a range between $340.40 and $342.50 all last week was strategic moves by option writers to defend the $340.00 option strike price which had attracted most buying interest.
Usually gold prices have edged lower after the expiry when option writers unload the positions bought as hedges against having to deliver on their option commitments.

Gold could respond to almost anything from the G7 now that it has been softened up by central banks reappraising their gold reserves and perceived threats of these stocks being reduced through selling into the market, dealers said.

A low-key statement after the talks made little impression on spot gold on Monday. The statement referred to the risks posed by currency volatility and the U.S. dollar promptly firmed against the yen and mark.

The most relevant weekend gold issue was at the World Bank/International Monetary Fund (IMF) meeting, also in Washington, on the possibility of the IMF selling five million ounces of the metal from its reserve.

Jack Boorman, director of the IMF's policy development and review department, said on Sunday the IMF hoped to use existing resources and bilateral contributions to fund its international debt relief plan for poor countries, but gold sales could be an option later.
This could mean selling five million ounces of IMF gold reserves, investing the proceeds and using the interest to fund the the Highly Indebted Poor Countries' (HIPC) programme.
"It's been discussed for months so it was hardly new but even the fact that it was talked about at the weekend will be worrying for the market," one analyst said.
Any efforts to contain the dollar strength and promote the yen, which was one interpretation of the G7 discussion, were dismissed as "hot air" by one analyst.
"How can you reduce strength in the currency of the only major economy in the world which is growing when the others are not?" the analyst said.
But he added, "Even if the talk is no more than rhetoric it might be favourable for gold (if the market expects action against the dollar)."
Palladium fixed at $161.50 last Friday, its highest level since May 31, 1995 and dealers estimated it had the potential to break $170.00 this week.
"It is very tight and nobody wants to be short as long as the Russians and Japanese are not talking," one dealer said.
Russia, the leading export of palladium and Japan, the major importer, have yet to discuss their 1997 supply contract.
No exports from Russia have come on to the market since last December, reducing palladium's availability in a tight dealer market.
--Brian Spoors, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8058
